content: Incisors, derived from the Latin word incidere, meaning to cut, are the first type of teeth found in heterodont mammals. These teeth are located in the premaxilla region of the jaw. In herbivorous and omnivorous mammals, such as humans and horses, incisors are specialized for sharp shearing. In contrast, in carnivorous mammals like cats, the incisors are relatively small and play a minimal role in food processing, as the primary function of biting off meat is performed by the canines and carnassials. In elephants, the upper incisors are uniquely adapted into curved tusks, while in narwhals, one of the upper incisors typically develops into a straight, twisted tusk. Rodents, on the other hand, have incisors that grow continuously throughout their lives and are kept in check by the act of gnawing. Humans typically have eight incisors, with two of each type: maxillary central incisors, maxillary lateral incisors, mandibular central incisors, and mandibular lateral incisors. Other animals, such as some primates, cats, and horses, possess twelve incisors. Rodents have four incisors, while lagomorphs (rabbits and hares) have eight, including a small pair of peg teeth located directly behind the most anterior pair. Rodent incisors are a key evolutionary adaptation that contributes to their success as a group. They have two incisors in the upper jaw and two in the lower jaw, separated from the molars by a toothless diastema region. The tissue of these incisors regenerates from the apical end and wears down at the distal tip due to constant use. These ever-growing incisors are divided into two regions: the crown analogue and the root analogue. The crown analogue represents the labial half of the incisor and is characterized by an enlarged cervical loop at the apical end, which serves as the epithelial stem cell niche. The epithelial progeny of this cervical loop differentiate into ameloblasts, which produce enamel. The root analogue, on the other hand, constitutes the lingual half of the incisor. Its cervical loop is smaller, and the epithelium does not differentiate into ameloblasts. Instead, it forms a root sheath and fragments into epithelial cell rests of Malassez, typical of root epithelium. The root analogue is covered in dentin and cementum, similar to a normal tooth root.
